description: Default private-term set inherited by an ordinary governed project. A project EXTENDS this in PROJECT.yaml; it never replaces it. This is a default, never a universal hard-coded list: a vocabulary built for one project silently fails to protect another.
applies_to: outgoing commit messages, branch and tag names, author and committer identities, repository paths, and blob content
tiering_rationale: Measured on a real project: four scan findings, zero true positives, one of which cost a history rebuild. `claude` matched Jean-Claude Martin in committed prose; `terra` matched Italian for 'ground'; `envelope` matched the ordinary English sense in a source comment. A rule that fires constantly on benign content does not merely annoy — it manufactures pressure to exempt whole directories, which is how a precise control becomes a hole. So bare common words apply where a person writes deliberately (commit messages, ref and tag names, identities, paths) and not to blob content, while distinctive multi-word terms apply everywhere. A worker name leaking in a commit message matters; matching it inside ordinary prose is noise.
optional_patterns_rationale: `\b[A-Z]{2,4}-\d{1,4}\b` is intended to catch ticket identifiers such as PROJ-123. Compiled case-insensitively on an ordinary Python project it matches utf-8, SHA-256, post-2011 and nearly every entry in a lockfile: measured at 7 findings, 0 true positives, on one project's first six commits. It is opt-in via private_terms.optional_pattern_groups, and a project adopting it should first verify it against its own tracked tree — the step that turned a noisy rule into a working one when this project derived its own identifier patterns instead (0 false positives, 1 true positive: a branch named for a capability).
generation_pattern_rationale: REPLACES THE LITERAL `gpt-5`, which aged the moment a new generation appeared: it matched `gpt-5.6-terra` and did not match `gpt-6-astra`, so the vocabulary silently stopped covering the models actually in use. A literal per slug means a release per slug, which is the failure this pattern exists to end. It sits in `patterns` rather than `identity_patterns` because that is the tier the literal was in, so coverage is generalised and not widened by tier. PRECISION IS THE CONSTRAINT, not an afterthought: it requires the vendor prefix AND a digit, so ordinary prose about the technology is untouched — `a GPT model`, `GPTs are useful`, `the ChatGPT subscription`, `Egypt-5`, `encrypt-5` and `gptcache` all scan clean, while `gpt-5`, `gpt-5.6-terra`, `gpt-6-astra`, `ChatGPT-5`, `gpt6`, `gpt_6` and a synthetic `gpt-7.1-vega` are all caught. Measured against a corpus in `test_scan_vocabulary.py::test_the_generation_pattern_*`, which also asserts it covers everything the literal covered. WHAT IT DOES NOT COVER, deliberately: a bare codename with no vendor prefix. `terra` already demonstrated why — it matched Italian for `ground` on a real project, which is the measurement the whole tiering rationale rests on, and a bare codename is an ordinary word in some language. Such a name is covered where it appears with its prefix and is otherwise a literal a project adds to its own vocabulary. A SPACE IS NOT A SEPARATOR HERE, and that is a correction rather than a choice: the first version allowed one, and an independent reader showed it firing on `I started using ChatGPT 2 years ago` — a quantity following a product name, which is ordinary English and exactly the class of false positive the tiering rationale above was written about. Removing the space costs the form `GPT 6`, which is prose spelling rather than a slug: every real identifier this surface publishes is punctuated or unseparated. The negative corpus in test_scan_vocabulary.py now carries that sentence.
